CONDS.info: Without gravity about 1.5–2 L of fluid moves toward the head. Pressure around the optic nerve rises, the back of the eye flattens and the optic disc can swell, giving a far-sighted shift. It affects roughly 70% of long-duration crew and grows with mission length.
act: Do the daily Amsler grid and near-vision card; report any new blur or distortion.
Wear the adjustable-focus (“superfocus”) glasses for a far-sighted shift.
Avoid long periods of straining, head-down positions and tight collars.
Ask the flight surgeon about thigh cuffs or lower-body negative pressure sessions if available.
Keep B-vitamin intake as planned and track cabin CO₂ (a known headache trigger).
CONDS.esc: Optic nerve sheath or retinal thickness above your trajectory, a far-sighted shift over 1 D, or headache with vision change: schedule OCT/ultrasound and send to the flight surgeon at the next pass.

CONDS.info: Blood volume falls 10–15% within days, the heart works against less load and slowly deconditions. Rhythm changes such as extra beats (PVCs) become more common on long missions. The main operational risk is fainting when gravity returns (landing, planetary surface, EVA).
act: Complete daily aerobic exercise (cycle/treadmill) plus resistance training.
Drink to plan; fluid- and salt-load before landing or a gravity transition as briefed.
Limit caffeine and check potassium/magnesium if extra beats rise.
Wear compression garments for re-entry and the first days in gravity.
CONDS.esc: QTc over 500 ms, resting heart rate over 130 bpm, fainting, chest pain or palpitations with dizziness: treat as urgent and contact the Crew Medical Officer (CMO) now.

CONDS.info: Weight-bearing bones (hip, spine) lose about 1–1.5% of their density each month without loading. Calcium released from bone raises urine calcium and kidney-stone risk within weeks.
act: Do high-load resistance exercise (ARED) 6 days a week; this is the most effective countermeasure.
Take vitamin D as issued (800–1000 IU/day) and keep calcium near 1000–1200 mg/day, not more.
Keep sodium moderate: high salt raises urine calcium.
Drink enough for over 2 L of urine a day to protect against stones.
Ask about potassium citrate or a bisphosphonate if turnover markers stay high.
CONDS.esc: Flank or back pain with blood in urine (kidney stone), urine calcium over 400 mg/day, or bone loss well ahead of trajectory: contact the flight surgeon.

CONDS.info: Crews average about 6 h of sleep against the 8.5 h scheduled, with less deep and REM sleep. Without a 24-h sunlight cycle the body clock drifts, which slows reactions and raises error risk.
act: Protect the 8.5 h sleep window and keep a fixed wake time.
Use bright, blue-rich light after waking and dim, warm light 2 h before sleep.
Use eye mask and ear plugs; keep the sleep station cool.
No caffeine within 6 h of sleep.
Ask the flight surgeon before using melatonin or a sleep medication.
CONDS.esc: Under 5 h of sleep for 3 nights or reaction-time lapses during critical tasks: tell the commander and flight surgeon so the schedule can be adjusted.

CONDS.info: Headward fluid gives the puffy face, stuffy nose and full-head feeling of early flight. Jugular veins swell; in some crew the flow slows or reverses, which can lead to a clot (seen in 6 of 11 crew studied; one had a thrombus).
act: Use saline nasal spray for congestion; keep the head of the sleep bag slightly raised.
Track headache, nasal congestion and facial puffiness in your symptom log.
Use thigh cuffs or lower-body negative pressure if issued.
CONDS.esc: Jugular flow that is stagnant or reversed, neck swelling or pain: urgent ultrasound review with the flight surgeon. Do not start blood thinners without ground direction.

CONDS.info: Postural muscles of the calf, thigh and back shrink 10–20% and lose 20–30% of strength over six months without heavy exercise. Strength falls faster than size.
act: Follow the resistance programme (ARED squats, heel raises, deadlifts) at prescribed loads.
Eat 1.2–1.5 g protein per kg body mass per day, spread over meals.
Log every session so the trend can be checked against your trajectory.
CONDS.esc: Strength down more than 20% from your trajectory or new back pain with numbness: tell the flight surgeon.

CONDS.info: Inactivity and stress hormones make muscle less sensitive to insulin. Glucose spikes after meals grow, fasting insulin rises and cholesterol can drift up on long missions.
act: Keep exercise volume up: it is the strongest insulin sensitiser.
Choose low-sugar menu items and pair carbohydrates with protein.
Check CGM traces after meals and log the food that caused spikes.
CONDS.esc: Fasting glucose over 126 mg/dL twice, glucose under 54 mg/dL, or HOMA-IR over 4: contact the flight surgeon.

CONDS.info: T-cell and natural-killer activity drops and inflammation markers rise. Dormant viruses (EBV, VZV, CMV, HSV) reactivate and are shed in saliva in about half of long-duration crew, sometimes causing rashes or cold sores.
act: Keep sleep, exercise and nutrition on plan; all three support immunity.
Use hand hygiene and clean shared surfaces.
Watch for cold sores, band-like rash (shingles) or persistent fever.
CONDS.esc: Fever with positive viral shedding, a new blistering rash, or lymphocytes under 1.0: contact the flight surgeon.

CONDS.info: Dry cabin air, limited washing and a changed skin microbiome cause dryness, rashes and slow-healing skin. Radiation adds to redness.
act: Moisturise daily with the issued emollient.
Use rinse-free cleansers gently; avoid scratching.
Take a weekly skin photo of the same spot for comparison.
CONDS.esc: Spreading rash, pus, or redness with fever: flight surgeon review.

CONDS.info: Galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events (SPE) damage DNA. Dose is tracked against the NASA career limit of 600 mSv and 30-day organ limits. A large SPE can give enough dose in hours to cause nausea and a drop in lymphocytes.
act: Follow storm-shelter procedures as soon as an SPE alert or dose-rate spike occurs.
Wear your personal dosimeter at all times.
Eat the antioxidant-rich menu items (fruits, vegetables, omega-3).
CONDS.esc: Dose rate over 5× expected (possible SPE): shelter now and tell the CMO. Nausea or vomiting within hours of a dose spike, or lymphocytes falling by half: medical emergency.

CONDS.info: The body destroys about 54% more red blood cells in space than on Earth, throughout the mission. Red cell mass falls ~10%, which can cause fatigue and lower exercise capacity, especially after landing.
act: Eat the full menu; do not take iron unless the flight surgeon prescribes it (iron stores rise in flight).
Pace exercise if unusually tired and log fatigue.
CONDS.esc: Hemoglobin under 12 g/dL, breathlessness or chest pain with exertion: contact the flight surgeon.

CONDS.info: Arteries stiffen in space at a rate similar to 10–20 years of ageing on Earth, measured as faster pulse-wave velocity and weaker flow-mediated dilation.
act: Keep aerobic exercise on plan.
Prefer omega-3 and polyphenol-rich foods; limit salt.
CONDS.esc: Pulse-wave velocity over 10 m/s or flow-mediated dilation under 4%: send to the flight surgeon.

CONDS.info: Crews often eat only 70–80% of what they need. Weight, muscle and bone loss follow, and stored food loses vitamins over time on long missions.
act: Eat to 100% of your energy target; log every meal.
Take vitamin D as issued.
Rotate menu items to avoid menu fatigue.
CONDS.esc: Body mass down more than 5%, or vitamin D under 20 ng/mL: contact the flight surgeon.

CONDS.info: Stress hormones (cortisol, ACTH) stay raised in flight and the daily cortisol rhythm flattens. Prolactin rises with stress and lost sleep; thyroid hormones shift slightly.
act: Use planned stress-relief: exercise, leisure, private calls home.
Protect sleep; it lowers cortisol and prolactin.
CONDS.esc: TSH or free T4 outside range, or cortisol over 3× your baseline: flight surgeon review.

CONDS.info: Early in flight the body sheds fluid; thirst is blunted and sodium handling changes. Dehydration raises kidney-stone risk and worsens orthostatic intolerance.
act: Drink to keep urine specific gravity under 1.020 (pale urine).
Keep salt moderate.
Re-check electrolytes after vomiting or heavy sweating.
CONDS.esc: Sodium under 130 or over 150 mmol/L, potassium under 3.0 or over 6.0 mmol/L: urgent flight surgeon contact.

CONDS.info: Healthy crew stay at 97–99% oxygen saturation in flight. A drop points to a cabin atmosphere fault (ECLSS), a suit issue or a lung problem.
act: Re-seat the probe and re-measure at rest.
Check cabin O₂ and CO₂ readings with the crew.
Use supplemental oxygen as per protocol if below 90%.
CONDS.esc: SpO₂ under 90%: emergency. Put on oxygen and alert the CMO and commander.

CONDS.n: Behavioural health (added: NASA HRP behavioural risk)
CONDS.info: Isolation, confinement, workload and delayed contact with home can lower mood, raise stress and slow thinking. NASA lists adverse behavioural conditions as a top risk for Mars missions. Not in the original sheets: added because the challenge names mood as an indicator.
act: Do the daily mood and stress check-in honestly.
Use private family and psychological conferences.
Schedule leisure, exercise and crew meals.
CONDS.esc: Mood 3 or lower for 3 days, or thoughts of self-harm: talk to the CMO now and request a private psychological conference.

VARS.how: Chest strap or wrist wearable; take a resting value after 5 min seated still.
Wearable morning reading lying still for 2 min.
Upper-arm cuff, seated (strapped in), arm at heart level, after 5 min rest.
Finger pulse oximeter; warm hands, keep still 30 s.
Forehead heat-flux (double sensor) patch, as used in the Circadian Rhythms study.
Continuous glucose sensor on the upper arm; fasting value before breakfast.
Segmental bioimpedance belt (upper vs lower body), measured at the same time each day.
Personal active dosimeter worn on the torso.
Wrist actigraphy; or log hours on waking.
Rate overall mood now, 1 = worst, 10 = best.
Scan food packages or log meals; baseline = your energy requirement.
Total minutes on treadmill, cycle and resistance device.
Dipstick or refractometer on first-morning urine.
Rebound tonometer (iCare); 3 readings per eye, report the mean of the higher eye.
Ocular ultrasound, 3 mm behind the globe, guided by ground if needed.
Onboard OCT scan of the optic disc region.
Near-vision card at fixed distance; enter the lens power needed to read the 20/20 line.
Look at the grid centre with each eye; 1 if lines look wavy or missing.
Estimated from bioimpedance and hematocrit trend.
Cardiac ultrasound or impedance cardiography at rest.
Stroke volume × heart rate (calculated by the device).
12-lead or wearable ECG at rest; device reports corrected QT.
Estimated from jugular/IVC ultrasound by protocol.
Neck ultrasound, left internal jugular, at rest.
Ultrasound of calf (soleus) and thigh at marked sites.
Dynamometer or resistance-device max test, same posture each time.
Space linear-acceleration mass device (SLAMMD) or scale in gravity.
Urine lateral-flow assay, run 3 times and enter the mean.
Breath CO analyser after 20 s breath-hold. Rises with red-cell destruction (Trudel 2022).
Projected from turnover markers in flight; DXA/QCT before and after.
Blood draw, flow cytometry (returned or on-board).
Lymphocytes from blood draw, imaging assay.
Blood draw; iron stores rise in flight.
Hourly saliva samples in dim light; shift vs preflight.
Formula from cumulative dose, or measured from a skin photo (camera input).

head.f: Controls sleep–wake rhythm, mood and reaction speed.

eyes.f: Focus light on the retina; the optic nerve carries the image to the brain.

neck.f: Jugular veins drain blood from the head; the thyroid sets metabolic rate.

lungs.f: Move oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out.

heart.f: Pumps about 5 L of blood a minute through the body.

blood.f: Red cells carry oxygen; the vessel lining controls flow and clotting.

abdomen.f: Digests food, stores energy and keeps blood sugar steady.

kidney.f: Balance water and salts; excrete calcium released from bone.

immune.f: Detects and fights infection; keeps latent viruses dormant.

bones.f: Supports the body and stores calcium; weight-bearing bones need load to stay dense.

muscle.f: Postural muscles of the legs and back keep you upright in gravity.

skin.f: Barrier against microbes and water loss.

whole.f: Radiation passes through all tissue and damages DNA.

F2.t: PNIF = Baseline PNIF × (1 − k × Fluid shift / 2.0 L), k = 0.35
F2.note: Your formula uses k = 1, which predicts ~88% loss of nasal airflow at the typical 1.75 L shift and would flag every crew member as critical. k = 0.35 gives a ~30% drop, closer to reported congestion. Editable in Reference.

F3.t: EMG strength = Baseline × (Muscle CSA / Baseline CSA)

F5.t: Hydration = Baseline − 4 AU per L fluid shift + 3 AU per °C temperature rise; pH = Baseline pH × (Na / Baseline Na)
F5.note: Penalty (4 AU/L) and bonus (3 AU/°C) coefficients were not given and are set here.

F5b.t: pH = Baseline pH × (Serum Na / Baseline Na)

F6.note: Safe threshold = NASA 30-day skin limit, 1500 mGy-Eq (≈ mSv here).

F8.t: PETCO = Baseline × (RBC mass / Baseline RBC mass) — replaced
F8.note: End-tidal CO rises when red cells are destroyed (heme breakdown releases CO). Trudel et al. 2022 measured a 54% increase in flight, so a falling RBC mass should not lower the CO estimate. End-tidal CO is measured directly by breath analyser and its expected course uses +30% (<30 d) and +54% (>30 d).

F10.t: Prolactin = Baseline × (Cortisol / Baseline cortisol) × (Habitual sleep / Sleep hours)
F10.note: Uses your own habitual sleep instead of a fixed 8 h, and caps the sleep ratio at 2.

F11.t: Phase angle = Baseline × (Muscle mass / Baseline) × (1 − Fluid shift / Total body water)
